replacement:
The special base <m>e</m> Why the defining limit exists

Here is a justification using completeness, the exponent laws, and the continuity of real powers already stated in . It does not use derivatives of exponentials, integrals, or infinite series.

Put F(x)=2^x. For any real u,v, the inequality (\sqrt{F(u)}-\sqrt{F(v)})^2\ge0 gives

F\!\left(\frac{u+v}{2}\right)=\sqrt{F(u)F(v)}\le\frac{F(u)+F(v)}2.

Repeated bisection gives the corresponding inequality at every fraction t=j/2^n between zero and one. Approximating any t\in[0,1] by these fractions and using continuity gives

F((1-t)u+tv)\le(1-t)F(u)+tF(v),\qquad 0\le t\le1.

For h>0, define S(h)=(F(h)-1)/h. If 0<h<k, apply the preceding inequality with u=0, v=k, and t=h/k. It gives S(h)\le S(k). Applying it at the point 0 between -1 and h gives F(h)\ge1+h/2. Consequently,

\frac12\le S(h)\le S(1)=1,\qquad 0<h\le1.

By completeness, c=\inf\{S(h):0<h\le1\} exists. Given \varepsilon>0, some h_0>0 satisfies S(h_0)<c+\varepsilon, and every 0<h<h_0 then satisfies c\le S(h)\le S(h_0)<c+\varepsilon. Thus S(h)\to c as h\to0^+, with 1/2\le c\le1. For the other side, the exponent law gives

\frac{2^{-h}-1}{-h}=\frac{S(h)}{2^h}\longrightarrow c\qquad(h\to0^+).

The two-sided limit therefore exists. Every a>0 has a unique expression a=2^r. Rescaling the input gives \lambda(a)=rc, including \lambda(1)=0. In particular, the unique base with \lambda(a)=1 is

e=2^{1/c}.

This proves that choosing the base by its slope at zero is possible and unambiguous.
reason: Close the unproved existence and uniqueness of lambda(a) and the special base e without using later integrals, power series, or chapter 6 convexity facts.
verification: Midpoint inequality follows from a square; dyadic approximation and known continuity give the displayed chord inequality. The chord inequality makes S increasing in h, bounds it in [1/2,1], and completeness yields its right limit. Exponential inversion gives the same left limit. Rescaling proves lambda(2^r)=rc and the unique e=2^(1/c).

replacement:
Square-root limit law

If f(x)\to L\ge0 as x\to a and f(x)\ge0 for all allowed x sufficiently close to a, then \sqrt{f(x)}\to\sqrt L. This includes limits approached only through the domain of the square root.

The estimate behind the rule is

|\sqrt u-\sqrt v|\le\sqrt{|u-v|},\qquad u,v\ge0.

For example, if u\ge v, then u-v=(\sqrt u-\sqrt v)(\sqrt u+\sqrt v)\ge(\sqrt u-\sqrt v)^2; interchange u and v for the other case. Thus making |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon^2 makes the square-root error less than \varepsilon. We will use this rule when rationalizing limits below.
